newsitem.title: FRANCE: France studies Cr Lyonnais recovery plan.
newsitem.headline: France studies Cr Lyonnais recovery plan.

text.p: The French finance ministry said on Tuesday it was studying a recovery plan submitted by Credit Lyonnais but had no comment on a report that the ailing bank was demanding another 12 billion francs ($2.3 billion) in state aid.
"We are studying the recovery plan and discussing with the bank various means" to help it out, a ministry official said.

The official said it was too early to say when the state- controlled bank's plan, aimed at readying it for privatisation, would be forwarded to the European Commission, which must approve any fresh public help. "We just received it at the end of last year and we are looking at it," the official said.
In Brussels a Commission spokesman said it might not rule on the new rescue before the bank's 1996 accounts were closed unless it knew more about the plan.
Credit Lyonnais, still trying to recover from an expansion binge that drove it to the brink of bankruptcy, has already obtained two state rescue packages.
The French daily Liberation said on Tuesday Paris might be ready to provide 12 billion francs in recapitalisation for the bank but a ministry spokesman declined comment on the article.
The centre-right government, which wants a fast sale of the bank, has pledged a third rescue package to get it in shape for privatisation but must decide on the sum it needs to inject.
Another source close to the case said no "formal request" had been made to the government for 12 billion francs.
If the figure is correct, it would bring the cost of state injections to the bank to more than 20 billion francs, or around 1,500 francs per taxpaying household.

The source said the figure in Liberation reflected comments by bank chairman Jean Peyrelevade last year that it would need a 12 billion franc capital boost to raise its tier one solvency ratio to six percent from 4.5 percent to attract buyers.
The average tier one ratio for French banks is six percent. It is seven percent for the European banking sector as a whole.
The Commission spokesman said on earlier on Tuesday that the Commission write to French representatives in Brussels saying it needed information quickly on new measures to aid the bank.
Otherwise, the Commission might not rule on the proposals by the end of March when the bank's 1996 accounts close. The plan had been expected to be unveiled with the bank's 1996 results.
Liberation said the new funds would be doled out in stages to the bank, which posted 21 billion francs in losses between 1992 and 1994, to stagger the impact on the state budget.

The government pumped 4.9 billion francs into the bank in the first rescue in 1994. A second bailout in 1995 hived off the bank's doubtful assets into a separate "bad bank". Last September, the government injected 3.9 billion francs into the bank to offset penalties imposed on the bank in the 1995 rescue.
The government has said the final bill will be evident only when losses on the sale of the bad assets are known. But analysts say the tally could hit at least 100 billion francs.

Liberation also said Brussels was unhappy about the bank's slow compliance with conditions it set in return for approving the 1995 state rescue. The bank was told to cut its European network by 35 percent but has only reduced it by 21 percent.

The ministry official reiterated the government's hopes of selling the bank fast but said there was no timetable. The bank has predicted it will not be ready for sale before 1998. ($1=5.280 French Franc)
